beats.text:
I push the empty ale mug aside, the ceramic scraping loudly against the scarred wood. Aldous and Zoe are too close, their voices sharpening like knives being honed, and if they keep this up, the tension is going to snap the very rafters of The Smoldering Hearth.

I need a distraction, something loud and bright to drown out the sound of their pride.

I plant my boots on the table, feeling the vibration of the tavern's low hum beneath the floorboards. I rise up, steadying myself against the hanging lantern until I'm standing tall above them, my skirts fluttering around my knees.

"Come on now, don't let the salt air spoil such a fine evening!" I belt out, forcing a grin that feels wider than it actually is.

I draw a deep breath, filling my lungs with the scent of spilled gin and damp wood, and let out a low, melodic note that climbs higher and higher, cutting through the argument until Zoe and Aldous are forced to look up.

Aldous reaches for the heavy iron poker leaning against the hearth, his eyes narrowing as he stares up at Lily. Zoe slams her palm against the table, causing the remaining liquid in her glass to slosh over the rim.

I let my hand stay pressed against the table, the spilled gin soaking into the wood and creeping toward my sleeve. The sudden, bright swell of Lily's voice is like a bucket of cold water thrown into a furnace, snuffing the heat of my temper before I can even decide if I'm angry or just exhausted.

"For heaven's sake, Lily, we aren't in a theater," I say, pulling my hand back and wiping the moisture onto my trousers. 

I look from Lily's wide, forced grin down to Aldous, who is still clutching that poker like he’s ready to defend the hearth from a siege. The tension hasn't vanished; it's just been shoved into the corners by the music.

The iron is cool and solid in my grip, a weight that anchors me while Lily's voice climbs toward the rafters. I stare up at her, my eyes tracking the way the lantern light catches the frantic brightness in her expression. She’s trying to bridge the gap between us with a melody, but all I can think about is how much more difficult it will be to bridge it once the song ends.

"It's a distraction, nothing more," I say, my voice sounding heavier and more tired than I intended.

I slowly lower the poker, the metal clinking softly against the stone of the hearth. The heat of the argument is still there, smoldering beneath the surface like the embers in the grate, but the sharp edge of our words has been blunted by her sudden, soaring note.

I catch the look in Aldous's eyes—that heavy, drowning sort of exhaustion—and it tugs at my chest, threatening to break my grin. He’s right, of course. This isn't a theater; it's a room full of ghosts and unpaid debts, and we are all just trying to keep from being swallowed by the dark.

"Then let it be a fine one!" I shout, abandoning the melody for a moment to lean down toward them, my hair brushing the rim of a half-empty mug. 

I don't give them time to argue, to let the silence settle back in like the damp. I pull the air deep into my lungs and launch into a bawdy sea shanty, the kind that makes you want to stomp your feet even when the world is falling apart. My voice rings out, loud and unrepentant, filling every crack and crevice of the back room until the only thing left to hear is the song.

I reach out, my fingers catching the edge of Lily's skirt to steady her, or perhaps to anchor her before she drifts too far into the rafters. The shanty is wonderful, truly, but it's too much—too bright, too loud, too much of a beacon for anyone listening in the main taproom.

"Lily, darling, save the encore for the docks," I whisper, leaning in close so my words are lost to her, though I know she can see the urgency in my eyes. "You'll have the whole of the wharf singing our business if you don't bring it down a notch."

I glance toward the door, my sergeant's instinct twitching in my gut. We aren't alone in this tavern, and the louder she gets, the more we invite the world to look in on us.

Lily abruptly cuts the shanty short, her grin faltering under Zoe’s urgent stare. A heavy, rhythmic thudding begins against the back door, as if someone is testing the weight of the wood with their heels.

I swallow the sudden lump in my throat, the shanty dying in my mouth as Zoe's hand anchors me. Her eyes are wide, frantic, and I realize that my performance is becoming a spotlight we can't afford to shine. The thudding at the door feels like a heartbeat, heavy and insistent, echoing the rhythm of my own pulse.

"Fine, fine, keep your secrets then," I murmur, the bravado dropping away to reveal the nerves humming beneath my skin.

I slide off the table, my boots hitting the floor with a muffled thud instead of a stomp. I don't go back to my seat; instead, I lean against the edge of the wood, staying close to Zoe and Aldous, trying to shrink myself into the shadows of the corner. I pick up a piece of dried bread from a nearby plate and begin to nibble on it, acting the part of a girl lost in a song, even as I watch the back door with one eye.

"But if they come knocking, I'm not the one explaining why we're all sitting in the dark looking like we've seen a ghost," I add, my voice barely a breath, low enough to stay between us but loud enough to keep the rhythm of our shared tension.

The thudding against the door isn't just a sound; it's a countdown. I can feel the vibrations in the soles of my feet, a heavy, rhythmic reminder that the world outside is no longer content to wait. Zoe's whisper is a sharp reality check, pulling me down from my high, bright perch and back into the dim, claustrophobic reality of the back room.

"If I don't get them to listen, Zoe, they'll be hearing us before we've even had a chance to hide," I murmur, my voice dropping to a conspiratorial hiss. 

I slide off the table, my knees feeling a little less steady than they did a moment ago. The bravado is still there, a thin layer of sugar over a bitter core, but the wide, theatrical grin has faded into something more jagged. I lean against the edge of the table, clutching the piece of bread like it's a lifeline, my eyes darting between the door and the shadows where Aldous stands.

I take a small, deliberate bite of the bread, trying to look like nothing more than a girl waiting for her next song, but my eyes keep drifting back to that door. The rhythm of the thudding is getting louder, more insistent, as if the wood itself is breathing.

"Just keep that iron close, Aldous," I say, casting a quick, nervous glance toward him. "Because if that door swings open, I don't think my next song is going to be a shanty."

The thudding at the door is no longer just a sound; it's a pulse, heavy and demanding, vibrating through the very soles of my boots. It's the sound of the outside world coming to collect, and my throat feels suddenly too small for the song I was just singing.

"Quietly, then. We wouldn't want to be too much of a nuisance," I whisper, the words catching slightly as I step down from my makeshift stage. 

I move away from the center of the room, sliding into the narrow, shadow-drenched space between the table and the heavy oak dresser. I keep my back to the wall, making myself small, trying to blend into the gloom like I belong there. My hands are trembling just enough that I have to hide them in the folds of my skirts, clutching the piece of bread as if it were a precious jewel rather than a dry scrap of crust.

I cast one more look at Aldous. He looks like a man waiting for a landslide, his knuckles white against the iron of that poker. 

"If they come through that door, Aldous, you better be ready to swing more than just a song," I breathe, my eyes fixed on the wood of the door as the rhythmic thudding grows more insistent, more certain.

The door doesn't just thud; it groans under the pressure of whatever is standing on the other side. The rhythm is too steady, too deliberate to be a drunk looking for a late supper. My heart is a trapped bird, fluttering against my ribs, and I can feel the sweat beginning to prickle at my hairline despite the chill of the room.

"I'm going, I'm going," I whisper, casting a quick, sheepish look at Zoe. 

I slide further into the shadows, my skirts whispering against the floorboards as I retreat toward the heavy oak dresser. The bravado is a thin, fraying thread now, and I am very much aware of how much space I'm taking up. I want to be invisible. I want to be nothing more than a trick of the light and a memory of a song.

I settle into the darkness, pulling my knees up slightly to keep my silhouette small, and watch the door. The wood seems to pulse with every heavy step from the hallway.

"If they're here for the debt, Aldous, we're going to need more than a song to pay it off," I murmur, my eyes never leaving the door, my voice barely a breath of salt and smoke.

The wood of the table is rough beneath my palms, smelling of spilled ale and old sawdust. I don't wait for the shouting to stop; I just make sure it can't be heard over the melody.

"Come on, boys, let's give the walls something better to listen to!" I belt out, my voice cutting through the tension like a knife through soft cheese. I find my footing, bracing my heels against the edge of the table so I can look Zoe and Aldous right in the eye.

I draw a breath, filling my lungs with the damp, salt-heavy air, and let out a low, trilling note that climbs until it hits the rafters. The song is old, something from the docks that everyone knows but nobody wants to sing when the debts are high.

The song takes flight, a jagged, salt-crusted thing that catches in the back of my throat before it spills out to meet the rafters. I pour everything into it—the hunger, the brine, the way the moonlight looks on the oil slicks in the harbor. Every time Zoe opens her mouth to bark a command or Aldous tries to squeeze a truth out of me, I just pitch the melody higher, turning the tavern into a cathedral of beautiful, desperate noise.

The argument dies. It doesn't even stand a chance against the swell of the chorus. I see the men at the bar stop their drinking, their eyes glazing over as the rhythm takes them, and I know I've won this round.

I stare at her, my jaw tightening until it aches. Just when I had her cornered, just when the truth was hovering on the edge of her teeth, she turns into a damn siren. The sudden wall of sound hits me like a physical weight, forcing the air from my lungs and shattering the focus I've spent the last hour building.

"Lily, for the love of the tides, shut it!" I snap, but my voice is a pebble tossed into an ocean of song. I slam my hand against the table, right next to her boots, but she doesn't even flinch. She just smiles, and that infuriating, bright, little liar's smile.

The melody is lovely, but it is a thief, and I have never liked thieves. It steals the gravity from the room, turning a reckoning into a celebration, and that is the most dangerous thing of all. I watch the way the light catches the condensation on my glass, waiting for the swell to dip so I can find my place again.

"A classic diversion," I mutter, though the sound is swallowed by the swell of the chorus. I look from the girl's swaying shoulders to the sergeant's reddening face, and I feel the weight of the ledgers in my mind. The music is loud, but the numbers in my head are louder, and they aren't singing.

I lunge forward, my fingers catching the hem of her tunic to steady her before she can dance herself right off the wood. The table groans under our combined weight, and I lean in close, my shoulder pressing against her hip to anchor her. I need her to hear me, and I need her to understand that the walls in this tavern have ears, and some of those ears belong to the harbor patrol.

"Lily, please," I hiss, the command losing its sharp edge and turning into something more desperate, more private. "Lower the volume before the whole docks comes knocking to join the chorus, and I've got nothing left to give them but a headache."

I cast a quick, sharp glance toward the door, then back to Aldous. He's too calm, too focused on his numbers, and if the noise doesn't settle, the weight of those ledgers is going to drop on all of us.

The tension in Zoe's grip is a sharp contrast to the soaring lightness of the melody, but I don't let it break my rhythm. I push the note higher, a desperate, shimmering thing that vibrates in my very teeth, making sure the eaves of the tavern catch it so the men in the street don't have a chance to hear the truth underneath. I feel the weight of Zoe's stare and the heat of her desperation, but I hold the note just a second longer, a shield of sound between us and the world.

"I hear you, Sergeant, I hear you," I breath-sing, the words catching on the tail end of a vibrato that keeps the room trapped in my spell.


I let the melody fall, letting the grand, crashing waves of the song recede into a soft, rhythmic murmur. I lean down slightly, bringing my face closer to Zoe's, the bravado draining out of my posture to make room for something more practical.

"Better?" I whisper, my voice barely a ghost of the power it had a moment ago. "We can't have the whole harbor knowing we're arguing over pennies and secrets."


The heavy oak door remains shut against the damp night air, and the thick, salt-stained walls of the tavern swallow the fading song. Outside, the docks remain quiet, save for the rhythmic slap of the tide against the pilings, leaving the three of them alone in their private, melodic sanctuary.
